title: Financial services: Investors urge Macquarie to focus on culture
full_text:
Macquarie investors say incoming chief executive Greg Ward should make an overhaul of the asset management and investment giant's governance and culture a priority after taking over from Shemara Wikramanayake later this year before turning his attention to the next phase of growth.
Macquarie announced the leadership handover at Thursday's annual meeting, continuing its long-standing tradition of promoting leaders from within. The firm, established as an offshoot of British investment bank Hill Samuel in 1969, has never appointed an external chief executive.
Australian Ethical head of Australian equities Nathan Parkin, whose firm oversees about $14 billion in savings, said Ward would inherit a business with a strong long-term outlook but one that first needed to address governance and regulatory issues that had weighed on investor sentiment.
"The focus should be on things like governance and cultures generally, and clearing the regulatory challenges that they have had," he said. "It's part of that internal focus broadly that we're talking about. That would be one of the issues, not the only one, but that would be one of the things that we would expect would be addressed."
Parkin said Macquarie's recent regulatory issues had largely centred on controls and disclosures, including matters involving futures trading, the electricity market and short selling.
"It's around controls and disclosures mainly, clearing those up will afford the business more freedoms. A focus on internal first will allow more options or optionality going forward."
He also pointed to shareholder concern over climate reporting, after almost one-fifth of investors voted against Macquarie's climate disclosures at this year's annual meeting.
Ward will take over as chief executive at a pivotal time for Macquarie, which faces scrutiny on several fronts, including over the handling of an investigation into alleged wrongdoing within its investment banking division.
Despite defending the bank's handling of a whistleblower matter involving the group's integrity office, Macquarie chairman Glenn Stevens said the board nevertheless continued to review whether there were "other things we can do to strengthen this process to make the responses that have been made more easily visible to people, so that there's better closure".
"We have a speak-up culture, so when people speak up through whatever channel that may be, and this was one, we listen to that," Stevens said.
"It has been thoroughly investigated through the processes that we normally would use for a whistleblower sort of event. I have confidence in the integrity of that process."
Ward, 58, succeeds Wikramanayake after she was eight years in the top job. Few investors expect him to make big changes to Macquarie's strategy after spending more than a decade transforming the banking and financial services division into one of the country's fastest-growing digital banks.
Having previously served as chief financial officer, Ward is widely credited with investing heavily in technology to build a digital banking platform that has steadily taken market share from Australia's major lenders.
His appointment also comes as financial institutions increasingly invest in artificial intelligence and digital capabilities, with investors expecting Macquarie to continue leveraging technology as a competitive advantage.
While Parkin wants management's early attention directed towards governance and regulatory matters, he remains optimistic about Macquarie's long-term growth prospects.
"They've got a very strong franchise in seeing trends early and backing themselves to make those capital allocation decisions," he said.
"They were early in data centres. I don't know what the next thing is, but we do know that the bench strength in the business is very strong, so we would expect that to continue."
Other institutional investors also expect continuity under Ward.
Sydney-based Airlie Funds Management, a money manager with $9 billion in assets, said Wikramanayake had left "a great legacy at Macquarie", with operating profit doubling to $6.7 billion during her tenure.
The fund manager said Macquarie promoted leaders from businesses where it saw the greatest future growth. Nicholas Moore came from investment banking before expanding the commodities and investment banking, franchises, while Wikramanayake grew asset management as well as banking and financial services.
"Greg's appointment follows his leadership of banking and financial services since 2013. To us, this indicates MQG sees significant growth runway in BFS," Airlie equity analyst Ray David said, adding Ward's language suggested he was unlikely to pursue transformational acquisitions while valuations in financial services remained elevated.
"Greg brings a rare combination to that role: the risk management pedigree of a GFC-era CFO, paired with the technology vision that transformed BFS into a digital leader," Investors Mutual analyst Joshua Frieman said, although he added that capital should be deployed if opportunities emerged.
